title: HTML Input Types
summary: The **`type`** attribute on `<input>` selects from a catalog of controls — `text`, `email`, `password`, `number`, `tel`, `url`, `date`, `checkbox`, `radio`, `file`, `range`, `color`, `search`, `hidden` — each with tailored UI, built-in validation, and (on mobile) a matching keyboard, configured by attributes like `placeholder`, `required`, `min`/`max`/`step`, and `pattern`.

subtopics.title: Text-like inputs: text, email, password, tel, url, search
subtopics.explanation: These share a text field UI but differ in semantics and validation. email validates an email format and shows an email keyboard; password masks characters; url validates a URL; tel doesn't validate (formats vary) but triggers a phone keypad; search may show a clear button. Picking the right one gives free validation and the correct mobile keyboard.

subtopics.title: Numeric inputs: number and range
subtopics.explanation: number gives a spinner field that accepts only numeric input and supports min, max, and step; range is a slider for the same constrained value when the exact number matters less than the relative position. Both clamp to min/max and snap to step. Use number for precise entry (quantity, age) and range for fuzzy selection (volume, brightness).

subtopics.title: Choice inputs: checkbox and radio
subtopics.explanation: checkbox is an independent on/off toggle — multiple can be checked, each submits its value only when checked. radio buttons sharing a name form a mutually exclusive group where exactly one can be selected. Use checkboxes for 'select any' and radios for 'select one of several'. Give each a value so the server knows which option was chosen.

subtopics.title: Date and color pickers
subtopics.explanation: type=date shows a native date picker and submits an ISO value (YYYY-MM-DD); related types include time, datetime-local, month, and week. type=color shows a color picker and submits a hex value (#rrggbb). These swap a fiddly text entry for a native, validated, locale-aware control with almost no code.

subtopics.title: File and hidden inputs
subtopics.explanation: type=file lets the user choose one or more files (add multiple for several, accept to filter types); the enclosing form must use enctype=multipart/form-data to upload. type=hidden holds a value the user doesn't see or edit (a CSRF token, a record id) that is still submitted with the form — useful for carrying state to the server.

subtopics.title: Validation attributes: required, pattern, min/max/step, value
subtopics.explanation: required blocks submission if empty; pattern enforces a regular expression; min/max/step constrain numeric and date ranges; maxlength limits text length; value sets an initial/default value. These trigger native constraint validation and bubble messages with zero JavaScript, though server-side validation is still mandatory.

subtopics.title: Mobile keyboard implications
subtopics.explanation: On touch devices the type changes the on-screen keyboard: email adds @ and a dot, tel shows a numeric keypad, url adds a slash and .com, number shows digits, search shows a Go/Search key. Choosing the right type (and inputmode for finer control) dramatically reduces typing friction and errors on phones.

subtopics.title: placeholder vs value vs label
subtopics.explanation: placeholder is grey hint text that disappears on input — it is not a label and must not replace one (it fails accessibility and vanishes while typing). value is the actual editable content/default. A real <label> names the field permanently. Use placeholder only for examples/format hints, never as the field's name.

foundations.overview: An <input> is one tag whose type attribute reshapes it into many distinct controls. Beyond the visual difference, each type carries built-in validation rules and, on mobile, a tailored keyboard. Combined with attributes like required, pattern, min/max/step, and placeholder, the right input type gives you a lot of correct behavior for free, reducing both code and user error.
foundations.formalDefinition: <input> is a void HTML element whose type attribute determines its data type, UI control, and built-in validation. Supporting attributes (placeholder, required, value, name, min, max, step, pattern, accept, multiple) refine its behavior and constraints.
foundations.whyItMatters: Choosing the correct input type improves data quality (validation), usability (right keyboard and picker), and accessibility, all with minimal code. It's a practical, frequently-tested skill in front-end work and interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of <input> as a Swiss Army knife: the type attribute picks which blade comes out — a text field, a number spinner, a slider, a date picker, a file chooser — and the other attributes set how sharp the constraints are.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser renders a type-specific control, applies constraint validation (type format, required, pattern, min/max/step) on submit, exposes the value in a normalized form (ISO date, hex color), and on touch devices selects the on-screen keyboard layout that matches the type and inputmode.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Signup forms (email, password), checkouts (number, tel, date), settings (checkbox, radio, color, range), uploads (file), and security/state (hidden) — virtually every form mixes several input types.
foundations.businessImpact: Right-typed inputs cut form-abandonment by reducing typing friction and validation errors, especially on mobile where the correct keyboard meaningfully improves completion rates — directly affecting conversions.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Native types deliver validation and specialized UI without custom JavaScript or third-party widgets, shrinking the codebase and the surface area for bugs while staying accessible by default.
foundations.performanceImpact: Native controls are lightweight and render instantly with no JS dependency, unlike heavy custom date/number widgets; this keeps bundles smaller and forms usable before scripts load.
commonUseCases: type=number with min/max/step for quantities and amounts
type=date / type=color for pickers without custom widgets
type=file with accept/multiple for uploads; type=hidden for tokens/ids

commonMisconceptions.myth: type=number guarantees only valid numbers reach the server.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Native validation can be bypassed (DevTools, scripts, disabled JS); client-side types improve UX but server-side validation is still mandatory.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A placeholder can serve as the field's label.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Placeholders are hints that disappear on input and aren't reliably announced by assistive tech; every control still needs a real <label>.

visualExplorer.title: Picking the right input type
visualExplorer.caption: A decision walkthrough from 'what data am I collecting?' to the type and attributes that fit.

config.intro: Each input type is tuned for a kind of data; matching the type to the data unlocks validation, the right keyboard, and the right picker.

steps.name: Free text?
steps.detail: Plain text → type=text; a known format like email/url/tel → use that type for validation and the right keyboard.

steps.name: A number?
steps.detail: Precise value → type=number with min/max/step; a fuzzy value on a scale → type=range slider.

steps.name: A choice?
steps.detail: One of several → radio group sharing a name; any of several toggles → checkboxes; one from a long list → a <select>.

steps.name: A date or color?
steps.detail: type=date (or time/month) for native, ISO-formatted dates; type=color for a hex color picker.

steps.name: A file?
steps.detail: type=file (add accept to filter, multiple for several) and set the form's enctype to multipart/form-data.

steps.name: Hidden state?
steps.detail: type=hidden carries a value (token, id) that's submitted but not shown or edited by the user.

interactiveExamples.title: A tour of common input types
interactiveExamples.explanation: Each control is the same <input> tag with a different type — note the distinct UI for number, range, date, color, and checkbox.

files.index.html:
<form>
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" placeholder="you@site.com"></label>
  <label>Quantity <input type="number" name="qty" min="1" max="5" value="1"></label>
  <label>Volume <input type="range" name="vol" min="0" max="100"></label>
  <label>Birthday <input type="date" name="dob"></label>
  <label>Theme color <input type="color" name="color" value="#3366ff"></label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="news" value="yes"> Subscribe</label>
</form>
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 20px; }
label { display: block; margin: 10px 0; }

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A form showing an email field, a number spinner, a slider, a native date picker, a color swatch, and a checkbox.

interactiveExamples.title: Validation attributes in action
interactiveExamples.explanation: required, pattern, and min/max trigger native validation messages on submit — no JavaScript needed. Try submitting empty or with a bad ZIP.

files.index.html:
<form>
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" required></label>
  <label>ZIP <input type="text" name="zip" pattern="\d{5}" title="5 digits" required></label>
  <label>Age <input type="number" name="age" min="18" max="120" required></label>
  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Submitting with an empty or invalid field shows a native error bubble; invalid fields get a red border.

interactiveExamples.title: Mobile keyboards via type and inputmode
interactiveExamples.explanation: On a phone, each type requests a matching keyboard. tel shows a keypad, email adds @, url adds .com and a slash. inputmode can override the keyboard without changing validation.

files.index.html: Open on a phone to see the keyboard change per field.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: On a touch device, each field summons a different keyboard (numeric keypad for tel, @-key for url, digits for the inputmode field).

debuggingLab.title: The number field accepts letters and out-of-range values
debuggingLab.symptom: A quantity field lets users type 'abc' and values like 0 or 999, and the wrong keyboard appears on mobile. The team thinks they used a number input.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 20px; }

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The field is type=text, so it accepts any characters, has no range, and shows the full keyboard on mobile. A text input has no numeric constraints at all — the type must be number (with min/max/step) to restrict input, validate the range, and request the numeric keyboard.
commonMistakes: Leaving inputs as type=text when a more specific type exists.
Using type=number but forgetting min/max/step so any number is allowed.
Relying on the type alone for security instead of validating on the server.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Change the field to type=number and constrain it with min, max, and step so only whole quantities in range are accepted.

theory.question: Why does the input type attribute matter beyond appearance?
theory.directAnswer: The type determines the control's UI, its built-in constraint validation, the normalized value format it produces, and — on touch devices — which on-screen keyboard appears. Picking type=email, tel, number, or date instead of generic text gives free format validation, a tailored keyboard, and native pickers, improving data quality and usability with no extra code.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The attribute that selects which kind of control an <input> becomes and what behavior it carries.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: HTML5 added specialized types so common data kinds get correct UI and validation natively instead of via custom widgets.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser renders a type-specific control, validates per the type's rules and any constraint attributes, normalizes the value, and on mobile maps the type to a keyboard layout.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right type is a quick win for UX, accessibility, and data quality and is commonly probed in interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: Switching a phone field from type=text to type=tel makes phones show a numeric keypad, cutting typos and speeding entry.

nestedTopics.title: Built-in validation
nestedTopics.explanation: type=email, url, number, date validate their format/range on submit automatically.

nestedTopics.title: Mobile keyboards
nestedTopics.explanation: type (and inputmode) select the on-screen keyboard, reducing typing friction.

nestedTopics.title: Normalized values
nestedTopics.explanation: date yields ISO YYYY-MM-DD, color yields #rrggbb, regardless of locale display.

followUps.question: Does the right type remove the need for server validation?
followUps.answer: No — client-side validation is bypassable; the server must always re-validate. The type improves UX, not security.

followUps.question: What's the difference between type and inputmode?
followUps.answer: type sets the control's semantics and validation; inputmode only hints the keyboard layout without changing validation, useful for text fields needing a numeric keypad.

theory.question: When would you use checkbox vs radio vs a select, and how do their values submit?
theory.directAnswer: Use radio buttons (sharing one name) when the user must pick exactly one of a small set; use checkboxes for independent on/off toggles where any number can be selected; use a <select> when picking one (or several with multiple) from a longer list to save space. Checkboxes and radios submit their value only when checked; an unchecked control sends nothing.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The set of choice controls and how their selections become form data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different selection patterns (one-of, any-of, one-from-many) need different controls for clarity and space.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Radios in a group share a name so only one's value submits; each checked checkbox submits its own name=value; a select submits the chosen option's value.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the wrong control confuses users and produces the wrong data shape; it's a frequent design and interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: Shipping speed (one choice) is radios; 'email me about X, Y, Z' (any) is checkboxes; country (long list) is a select.

nestedTopics.title: Shared name for radios
nestedTopics.explanation: Radios become mutually exclusive only when they share the same name.

nestedTopics.title: Checked submits value
nestedTopics.explanation: Only checked boxes/radios contribute to form data; unchecked send nothing.

nestedTopics.title: select vs radios
nestedTopics.explanation: Few visible options → radios; many → a space-saving select.

followUps.question: How do you submit multiple checkbox values under one key?
followUps.answer: Give the checkboxes the same name (often name="opts"); each checked one submits opts=value, which servers collect as a list.

scenario.question: Mobile users complain that your checkout form is painful to fill: the phone field shows a full keyboard, the card field shows letters, and the date field is a free-text mess. How do you improve it?
scenario.directAnswer: Match each field's type to its data: type=tel for the phone (numeric keypad), type=text with inputmode=numeric (and a pattern) for the card so it shows digits but allows formatting, and type=date for the date to get a native picker and ISO value. These changes summon the right keyboard and validate format with essentially no JavaScript, sharply reducing mobile friction.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A mobile usability fix driven by correct input types and inputmode.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Touch devices pick the keyboard from the type/inputmode, so the wrong type means the wrong keyboard.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: type=tel and inputmode=numeric request numeric keypads; type=date provides a native picker; each reduces taps and errors.

scenario.whyImportant: Mobile form friction is a leading cause of checkout abandonment, making correct typing a real business lever.

nestedTopics.title: inputmode
nestedTopics.explanation: Hints the keyboard for text fields without changing validation (e.g., numeric for card numbers).

nestedTopics.title: Native date picker
nestedTopics.explanation: type=date replaces error-prone free text with a validated, localized picker.

followUps.question: Why not just use type=number for the card?
followUps.answer: type=number strips leading zeros, allows spinners and exponents, and rejects spaces/dashes used for grouping — text + inputmode=numeric is safer for formatted IDs like card and ZIP codes.

coding.question: Write a signup form using the most appropriate input types: full name, email, password, age (18+), birthday, a favorite-color picker, a profile photo, and a hidden CSRF token.
coding.thoughtProcess: Map each field to its best type: text for name, email for email (validation + keyboard), password to mask, number with min for age, date for birthday, color for the picker, file with accept for the photo (so set enctype), and hidden for the token. Add names and required where appropriate.

solution.code:
<form action="/signup" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="abc123">

  <label>Name <input type="text" name="name" required></label>
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" required></label>
  <label>Password <input type="password" name="password" minlength="8" required></label>
  <label>Age <input type="number" name="age" min="18" max="120" required></label>
  <label>Birthday <input type="date" name="dob"></label>
  <label>Favorite color <input type="color" name="color" value="#3366ff"></label>
  <label>Profile photo <input type="file" name="avatar" accept="image/*"></label>

  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

coding.lineByLine: The form posts as multipart/form-data because it contains a file input. The hidden CSRF field submits a token the user never sees. type=email/password/number/date/color/file each provide tailored UI and validation; min=18 enforces the age floor, minlength=8 the password length, and accept=image/* filters the file chooser. Every control has a name so it's submitted.

alternativeApproaches.title: Add inputmode for fine keyboard control
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For text fields that hold digits (like a formatted phone or card), keep type=text but add inputmode=numeric to summon the numeric keypad without number-input quirks.

followUps.question: Why does this form need enctype=multipart/form-data?
followUps.answer: It includes a file input; only multipart/form-data can carry the file's binary contents, whereas the default urlencoded sends just the filename text.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Standardize a mapping from data kind to input type (email→email, phone→tel, quantity→number+min/max, date→date) and bake it into form components so every field gets correct validation and keyboards by default rather than ad hoc per-form decisions.
productionDeepDive.performance: Native types render instantly and need no JavaScript, avoiding heavyweight custom date/number/color widgets that bloat bundles; this keeps forms fast and usable before scripts hydrate.
productionDeepDive.security: Treat all client-side type and constraint validation as UX only — it's trivially bypassed. Re-validate and sanitize every value server-side, scan and limit uploaded files (type, size), and use hidden inputs for tokens like CSRF, never for trusted authorization data the client could tamper with.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Encapsulate inputs in a design-system Field component that accepts a type and constraint props, so hundreds of forms across teams stay consistent, accessible, and correctly typed without copy-paste drift.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Leaning on native types and attributes (required, pattern, min/max) keeps validation declarative in markup rather than scattered across JavaScript, making forms easier to read and change.
productionDeepDive.observability: Track per-field validation failures and correction rates to spot poorly chosen types or unclear constraints, and monitor mobile completion rates to confirm the right keyboards are improving conversion.

caseStudies.problem: High cart abandonment on phones due to wrong keyboards and free-text dates.
caseStudies.solution: Audited every field and assigned the correct type/inputmode plus native date pickers.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Minor visual inconsistency across OS-native pickers in exchange for far lower friction.
caseStudies.lessons: Input type is a cheap, high-leverage UX fix — especially on mobile where keyboards make or break completion.

Which inputs only submit a value when 'checked', and why?

keyTakeaways: The input type attribute reshapes <input> into a catalog of controls (text, email, password, number, tel, url, date, checkbox, radio, file, range, color, search, hidden), each with its own UI and validation.
Attributes like required, pattern, min/max/step, maxlength, and value drive native constraint validation without JavaScript — but the server must still validate.
The right type chooses the mobile keyboard (tel→keypad, email→@, url→.com); inputmode fine-tunes the keyboard for text fields.
Checkboxes and radios submit their value only when checked; radios sharing a name are mutually exclusive; hidden inputs submit values the user can't see or edit.
type=file needs enctype=multipart/form-data; placeholders are hints, not labels — every control still needs a real <label>.
